title: India's First Private Rocket Is Ten Days From Orbit. The Startup Behind It Just Became a Unicorn.
excerpt: Skyroot Aerospace has set a July 12 launch window for Vikram-1, aiming to become only the fourth private company in the world to place a satellite in orbit from its own launch vehicle.
body:
Somewhere on the Andhra Pradesh coast, at the same launchpad that has sent Indian satellites to the Moon and Mars, a seven-storey rocket built entirely by a private startup is standing upright, waiting for its moment.

Skyroot Aerospace announced on Thursday that it has set a launch window of July 12 to August 4 for its Vikram-1 rocket — a mission it has named *Aagaman*, meaning "arrival." If it succeeds, it will be the first time an Indian private company has placed a satellite in orbit, and only the fourth such achievement globally, after SpaceX, Rocket Lab, and Firefly Aerospace.

## From ISRO Labs to a Billion-Dollar Bet

Skyroot was founded in 2018 by two former ISRO scientists, Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka, in Hyderabad. Their pitch was simple and audacious: build rockets faster and cheaper than government agencies, and sell rides to space for the world's growing fleet of small satellites.

The company proved it could fly in November 2022, when its suborbital demonstrator, Vikram-S, became the first privately built rocket launched from Indian soil. That test validated the core technology stack. What comes next is vastly more complex.

Vikram-1 is a four-stage, multi-stage launch vehicle roughly 20 metres tall and 1.7 metres in diameter. The first three stages use solid propulsion; the upper kick stage runs on a liquid engine for precise orbital insertion. The airframe is built with carbon-composite structures to minimise weight. Skyroot says the vehicle can carry payloads of up to 350 kilograms to low Earth orbit — the sweet spot for the booming small-satellite market.

In May, the company raised $60 million from GIC and Sherpalo Ventures, pushing its valuation past $1.1 billion and making it India's first space-tech unicorn. Other backers include Temasek and funds managed by BlackRock.

## A Partially Commercial Flight

"With Vikram-S in 2022, we validated the foundation of our technology stack. With Vikram-1, we take our biggest step yet toward a reliable, high-cadence launch programme built in India, for India and the world," said Naga Bharath Daka, co-founder and COO.

The test flight will carry a mix of domestic and international payloads. While the primary objective is to collect in-flight performance data across propulsion, guidance, and stage separation systems, the commercial payload component signals confidence. Skyroot plans to begin full commercial operations after one or two successful demonstration flights.

As of July 1, all four stages had been integrated and stacked at the launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota. Prime Minister Narendra Modi had unveiled the flight-ready configuration of Vikram-1 in November 2025 during the inauguration of Skyroot's Infinity campus in Hyderabad.

## Why It Matters Beyond the Launchpad

Skyroot is competing in a global market for small-satellite launches that is projected to grow to $32 billion by 2031, driven by demand for Earth-observation constellations, IoT connectivity, and defence surveillance. Currently, Rocket Lab dominates this segment, with SpaceX's rideshare programme as the low-cost incumbent.

India's advantage is cost. The country already offers some of the cheapest launches in the world through ISRO's commercial arm, NewSpace India Limited. Private entrants like Skyroot and Agnikul Cosmos could push prices even lower, while offering the rapid turnaround times that constellation operators demand.

The government is betting big on this transition. India's space economy target is $44 billion by 2033, and the sector has been progressively opened to private players since 2020. Industrial heavyweights like Larsen & Toubro and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited have begun manufacturing PSLV rockets under contract from ISRO, while dozens of smaller startups are building everything from satellite buses to propulsion systems.

## The Diaspora Connection

For Indian-origin investors and technologists in the US and beyond, India's private space sector represents a rare convergence: deep engineering talent, government backing, cost advantages, and a regulatory framework that — unlike many countries — actively encourages private launch activity.

Skyroot's investor roster already reflects this. GIC (Singapore's sovereign wealth fund) and Sherpalo Ventures (the investment vehicle of Google chairman John Doerr's co-investor Ram Shriram, an Indian-American tech pioneer) both participated in the latest round.

The next ten days will determine whether India's private space ambitions remain a promise or become a proven capability. If Vikram-1 reaches orbit, Skyroot won't just be India's first private launch company — it will be proof that the country's startup ecosystem can compete at the frontier of deep tech, not just in software.
